paras: The lynching of Ed Berry was the hanging of a Black man by masked men in Shawnee, Oklahoma, early on August 6, 1915, after he was taken from a deputy sheriff who was bringing him to trial. Berry was charged with criminal assaults on white women, and a coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of a mob of persons unknown. A Shawnee dispatch calling it "one of the most orderly lynchings in the history of the state" was repeated in white and Black papers across the country.

The Associated Press said Berry was charged with two cases of criminal assault and suspected in ten others committed in Shawnee over three years, while United Press and the Guthrie Daily Leader said he was accused of killing two women. The Tulsa Daily World tied his arrest to an assault on a white woman on the night of July 11, traced through a mutilated half-dollar. Because officials feared he would be lynched amid "general indignation" over delays, he had been moved from place to place and lodged in the penitentiary at McAlester; his case was set for August 9.

Deputy Sheriff Gus Mitchell brought Berry back to Shawnee by train, and when the two alighted before dawn about a dozen masked men covered the deputy with revolvers and disarmed him. Ten or twelve automobiles of masked men then took Berry to Beard Street beside the Santa Fe railway bridge, described as the scene of one of the crimes attributed to him. With a rope around his neck he was questioned about the crimes, and according to the wire account he nodded each time he was asked whether he was guilty.

He was then hanged from a telephone pole in the presence of about 75 men, all masked, who dispersed quietly. Roundup accounts based on Shawnee dispatches added that the mob riddled his body with bullets.

A coroner's jury met that afternoon and found that Berry died at the hands of a mob composed of parties unknown to the jury, which the Montgomery Advertiser described as an open verdict. The Guthrie Daily Leader reported that scores viewed the unclaimed body, that the sheriff's officers had no trace of any member of the mob, and that prosecution of the lynchers "would not be popular in Shawnee." No arrests were reported, and the governor's office said it had not yet received an official report.

On the night of Saturday, August 7, unknown persons exploded a stick of dynamite under the Black church at nearby Wellston. The Oklahoma City Times called the blast "an echo of the lynching" and reported "considerable race feeling" in the region.

The Associated Press story, printed from Connecticut to Florida, led with the alleged confession and stressed that "in every case the negro's victim was a white woman." The United Press version had Berry confessing to killing two women, and the Chickasha Daily Express headlined it "Slayer Is Lynched." Oklahoma papers adopted the mob's view most fully: the Guthrie Daily Leader described "an orderly crowd of determined citizens," and the Oklahoma City Times called Berry "the negro ravisher."

A Memphis roundup the next day placed the lynching among nine Black men hanged in the South in one day, beside the lynching of Will Leach at Trilby, Florida. Some papers read the "orderly" dispatch with irony: the Milwaukee Leader headed its paragraph "An 'Orderly Mob,'" and the Richmond Virginian said the dispatches "ingenuously" told the story. Editorials divided, with the Lowell Sun counting the Oklahoma lynching among "American atrocities" and the Atlanta Jeffersonian holding that such crimes "deserved death."

No Black paper in the coverage printed an original report; the Chicago Defender reprinted the Memphis roundup as "Nine Human Beings Hanged in South Within 24 Hours," calling five of the deaths "Cold Blooded Murders," though its text garbled Berry's name as "Emily." The Denver Star reprinted the Defender item, and the Cleveland Gazette reprinted a Cleveland Plain Dealer editorial, "An Uncivilized State," that named the Oklahoma death a lynching but aimed its sharpest words at a public legal hanging in Mississippi.

The Guthrie Daily Leader's first report said the mob demanded Berry at the jail and rushed the sheriff when he refused, and a weekly news summary also said he was "taken from jail"; the more detailed wire accounts, which name the deputy, place the seizure at the train. The confession rests on the lynchers' side alone: the AP said Berry nodded, while the Guthrie paper said he admitted two killings, boasted of twenty other attacks, and gave a written confession, "it is said."

accounts.label: United Press wire
accounts.gist: Berry, accused of killing two women, was said to have confessed and was lynched by a mob that took him from officers, at the scene of one of his crimes; hanged to a tree.

accounts.label: Guthrie Daily Leader special
accounts.gist: An 'orderly crowd of determined citizens' rushed the sheriff at the jail without a shot and hanged Berry to a tree after he admitted two killings and boasted of twenty attacks.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Berry came to his death at the hands of a mob composed of parties unknown to the jury.

accounts.label: Memphis roundup
accounts.gist: One of nine Black men hanged in the South in a day; Shawnee dispatch called it one of the most orderly lynchings in the state's history, the body riddled with bullets.

framing.detail: AP headlines such as 'Mob Hangs Negro to Telephone Pole' and 'Negro Admits Crimes, Lynched in Oklahoma' stressed the confession and that every victim was a white woman.
Oklahoma papers called the lynchers 'an orderly crowd of determined citizens' and Berry a 'notorious negro' and 'the negro ravisher'.
The Milwaukee Leader's 'An "Orderly Mob"' and the Richmond Virginian's 'ingenuously' read the 'orderly' dispatch with irony; the South Bend News-Times favored legal hanging over lynching.
The Lowell Sun, reprinted in New Hampshire, listed the Oklahoma lynching among 'American atrocities'.
The Atlanta Jeffersonian said the week's lynchings followed crimes that 'deserved death'.
The Chicago Defender headed the roundup 'Nine Human Beings Hanged in South' and called five deaths 'Cold Blooded Murders'.
The Cleveland Gazette reprinted the Plain Dealer's 'An Uncivilized State', calling lynchings vicious and degrading but aiming chiefly at Mississippi's public hanging.
The Denver Star reprinted the Defender roundup with the 'most orderly lynchings' quote.
